# Meridian personas and user journeys

Meridian helps people research questions, build account knowledge and develop guidance they can use and revise through experience. In consulting work, that knowledge carries into discovery, assessment, scope, commercial decisions and delivery. Recommendations and commitments remain connected to their evidence, responsible people and accepted versions.

These roles and journeys are proposals to validate. Meridian has not been rebuilt; the current local interactive walkthrough uses simulated agent responses and saves work in the browser.

## Knowledge steward

Develop and maintain reusable guidance

When a recurring question or unexpected result challenges our guidance, I want to compare methods, research and counterexamples so the next person can understand the recommendation and when it applies.

Design proposal: Give shared knowledge a research, conversation and document context in Knowledge & agents. Collect evidence throughout work and review exceptions as they arise, as well as at project closeout.

Validation: Ask a knowledge steward to reconstruct the last change to an offering: what prompted it, which counterexample mattered, who used it next, and what made it trustworthy. Test who owns the research and what should trigger a review.

### Frame the knowledge gap

Goal: Name the question to answer.

Proposed: Open a question about a method, market or offering; select reusable sources and record the intended audience.

Decision: Can existing guidance answer this, or is research needed?

Handoff: Steward → Surveyor/Researcher: bounded question, audience and source scope; accept a research plan with explicit unknowns.

Recovery: If no usable sources exist, save the question and draft assumptions for further research.

### Test the idea

Goal: Distinguish a useful explanation from a plausible story.

Proposed: Compare research with recorded experience, preserve conflicting claims and ask questions that would materially change the guidance.

Decision: Which claim is supported, contradicted or still a working assumption?

Handoff: Researcher → steward: candidate advice and counterevidence; accept only the scope the evidence supports.

Recovery: On inaccessible or stale sources, show the gap, retain successful findings and continue with qualified advice.

### Make guidance usable

Goal: Explain where the recommendation should and should not be used.

Proposed: Save a version of the guidance with its conditions, examples, exclusions and next review trigger; routine private refresh follows policy.

Decision: Reuse privately, narrow, pause or keep investigating?

Handoff: Steward → account/solution lead: version and applicability; receiver can explain the conditions without reopening the whole research task.

Recovery: If evidence changes, mark affected guidance for reassessment and preserve prior uses and accepted work.

### Learn from later use

Goal: Improve the advice from actual results and corrections.

Proposed: Collect eligible actual results and conversations during work; compare them with the original prediction, ask about unresolved causes and retain counterexamples.

Decision: Change applicability, change advice, retire it or leave the outcome unresolved?

Handoff: Delivery lead → steward/Researcher: result with scope and alternative explanations; return revised advice to the next permitted use.

Recovery: Keep unreviewed findings marked as unreviewed. If interpretation fails, create a review item and leave the result unresolved.

## Account lead

Research and maintain account knowledge

When an organization or existing account becomes relevant, I want to understand its business, relationships and likely needs so I can decide whether and how we could help.

Design proposal: Save research and decisions at account level. An account lead can create a pursuit when they choose to develop a potential client engagement and carry the relevant knowledge into it.

Validation: Ask an account lead for the last research task that did not lead to a deal. What remained useful, where was it kept, and what later reopened the question? Test how they distinguish a potential client engagement from a pursuit they have chosen to develop.

### Start with a subject

Goal: Identify the organization or account the question concerns.

Proposed: Find or create an account identity and state the business question; use relevant shared knowledge as a starting point.

Decision: Existing account, separate subject or ambiguous match?

Handoff: Account lead → Surveyor: subject and purpose; result must resolve to the intended account or stay unlinked.

Recovery: Hold ambiguous identities separately and ask for a distinguishing fact before merging names.

### Build an understanding

Goal: See what is known, assumed and missing.

Proposed: Combine public research, authorized relationship history and shared expertise into an account-level view; keep inference editable and sources available on request.

Decision: Which need is plausible enough to investigate, and which claim changes the next conversation?

Handoff: Surveyor/Cartographer → account lead: attributed findings and uncertain links; receiver can correct the understanding.

Recovery: Mark missing connections as incomplete coverage and retain conflicting claims for clarification.

### Choose whether to act

Goal: Select a proportionate next action.

Proposed: Compare possible help with available capabilities; choose further research, monitoring, relationship contact, no fit or a pursuit.

Decision: Is there enough reason to pursue specific work?

Handoff: Account lead → solution lead only if pursuing: need, evidence, alternatives and open questions; keep the originating account question.

Recovery: If the need is contradicted, retain the learning at account level and choose no pursuit.

### Keep the account useful

Goal: Preserve understanding for the next relevant event.

Proposed: Save the decision, rationale and revisit condition at account level; carry relevant context into a new deal while keeping the account’s history in place.

Decision: What change should cause another look?

Handoff: Account lead → next account owner: current understanding and next question; receiver can resume without reconstructing the relationship.

Recovery: If a source changes, show the change and affected assumptions; preserve accepted commitments elsewhere.

Recommend Option A for this quarter’s priority: finding existing inspection reports during the November review cycle. It adds a searchable index to the current archive, which remains the source of record. The proposed fixed fee is $24,000, with delivery estimated at four weeks after written approval and access to the archive export. Both prerequisites remain outstanding. November use depends on when they arrive; no completion date has been promised.

The index covers equipment number and inspection date already in document metadata. It excludes extracting missing fields from scans and correcting inaccurate metadata. In the 120-report sample, 97 had both fields; we do not know whether that sample represents all 18,000 reports. Reports with missing metadata will not be searchable by the missing field. Review the missing-field report before deciding on a separate cleanup. Search-time savings remain unmeasured because there is no baseline.

Defer Option B, which replaces the archive, to a separate decision. Its proposed implementation fee is $78,000 plus an unquoted annual subscription, with implementation estimated at twelve weeks after the same prerequisites. Retention workflows, reviewer assignments and version comparison are outside the analysts’ requests for November. The estimate excludes migration of historical annotations, and Legal has not assessed the new system’s retention requirements.

At tomorrow’s meeting, seek the sponsor’s decision on Option A and establish when written approval and archive-export access can be provided. Neither option is approved; this recommendation is not a purchase order.

# Save filters for your shipment table

Saved filters are now available to paid-workspace users in the web app. Set your shipment status, destination and planned dispatch date filters, then choose **Save filter** and give the combination a name.

Select a saved filter from your filter menu to apply those values again. You can rename or delete your saved filters. Each name must be unique within your workspace.

Saved filters are personal to you and cannot be shared with your team in this release. They leave shipment records and other people’s tables unchanged. You can still filter the table without saving.

Saved dates are fixed calendar dates: a filter for 1–7 November will still use 1–7 November next week. Saved filters are not yet available in the mobile app.
